#1516. Mauricio Pochettino is adored by his players, big on culture and good vibes, not afraid to crack the whip and does not suffer fools - exactly what dysfunctional Man United are crying out for

By KIERAN GILL, MAIL SPORT REPORTER and MATT BARLOW, FOOTBALL WRITER and DANIEL MATTHEWS, US SENIOR SPORTS WRITER

Published: 17:59 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 18:01 EST, 10 November 2026

After one press conference during Mauricio Pochettino’s ill-fated spell at Chelsea, he hosted an Argentinian-style BBQ for approximately 130 people, including his players and their families, under a marquee set up in the first-team car park at their training ground.

Returning to the room and the assembled throng of journalists still working, Pochettino popped a large plate of sausages and steaks down on the desk. He insisted it did not constitute bribery for better coverage of him. Just thought we might like to join.

This was Pochettino personified. Big on togetherness. Insisted on creating a homely environment for everyone. Believed a harmonious culture at Cobham would help performances on the pitch. Even kept a big box of lemons in his office because he reckoned they harnessed ‘energia universal’. He emphasised the importance of a good mood.

Goodness knows that’s what Manchester United need right now. And if they do decide to dismiss Michael Carrick, the prospect of managing possibly the biggest club in world football would not faze Pochettino – now the bookies’ favourite to take over.

Indeed, the 54-year-old would relish the challenge.

A few days before USA’s World Cup victory against Bosnia and Herzegovina to reach the last 16 at this summer’s tournament, coach Pochettino invited a small group of journalists to interview him at the team hotel – the Ritz-Carlton in Laguna Niguel, overlooking the Pacific Ocean 50 miles south of Los Angeles.

Manchester United could do with a dose of Mauricio Pochettino - and he would relish the challenge

The United States manager - who would cost around £7.5million to release - has openly admitted he wants to lead them in the future

Towards the end of the interview the Manchester United job came up in conversation. Pochettino turned to his long-time assistant coach Jesus Perez and said: ‘One day, your dream comes true... you go to Manchester United!’.

The Argentine clarified somewhat by explaining that Perez, while living in London, would often visit Manchester on days off to visit the National Football Museum. Perez responded with a smile: ‘United should have got you’.

One thing about Pochettino that Manchester United players will soon figure out if he takes the reins at Old Trafford is that he is not afraid to crack the whip and does not suffer fools. At the World Cup, he appeared to criticise the intervention of FIFA - and President Trump – in suspending Folarin Balogun’s ban to make the striker available for a knockout clash with Belgium.

‘I feel disappointed with too many people. They put politics and manipulation, talk about ethics and integrity [first]. If we talk about the history of this game, I am disappointed in a personal way.’

With Pochettino, you’re either all in or you’re out. Look back to his time at Tottenham for evidence of that: the decision to exile stars such as Younes Kaboul, Etienne Capoue and Paulinho into a ‘bomb squad’ - and give chances to stars such as Harry Kane - was the start of his success there.

He’s a builder of teams, works with the tools he has and makes players better. Again, that sounds like the sort of thing United are crying out for.

Pochettino is big on culture – he adopted the mantra ‘culture eats strategy for breakfast’ after a meeting with the chairman of U.S. fast food chain Chick-fil-A – and worked hard to change the holiday camp feel at the USA team. Senior stars believed they did not need to put in the extra work to keep their places. The most notable example saw national team poster-boy Christian Pulisic, once of Chelsea, attempt to skip key games after a long season for AC Milan. Pochettino put a stop to that.

The Argentine does not suffer fools, is big on culture, and can deal with big club executives - his time at Tottenham taught us that

He can manage upwards, too. He handled chairman Daniel Levy well, and credited open dialogue as being key to the partnership with the chairman which yielded a runners-up finish in the Premier League and a run to the Champions League final.

‘I speak to him a lot, we talk a lot, we have very good communication,’ Pochettino said in 2018.

‘That means sometimes we agree and sometimes we don't agree. But after, when the decision is made, we are so strong in the delivery of it which shows it is best for the club’.

His cordial relationship with Levy meant Spurs were unconcerned when he met Sir Alex Ferguson in 2016 at Scott’s in Mayfair towards the end of Louis van Gaal’s troubled reign at Old Trafford.

There was nothing untoward in that - after the restaurant meeting Pochettino returned to Spurs training, and United appointed Jose Mourinho that summer.

But he was again touted as a contender when Mourinho was dismissed two years later.

Levy sacked him in 2019, but Pochettino has remained respectful and has since praised Levy’s impact.

On the field, his time at Spurs became famous for relentless intensity - a high energy approach with a high press. Think flying full-backs Danny Rose and Kyle Walker, and all-action midfielder Mousa Dembele. For another example of him getting the best from players look at Cole Palmer. The Englishman has never since replicated his numbers from 2023-24, Pochettino’s only season at Stamford Bridge.

The football, admittedly, was a little chaotic at Chelsea. It lacked control, and not even a mountain of meat could prevent him from being quizzed about his style of play in press conferences.

Chelsea’s fans never took to Pochettino. He was the face of Spurs, after all. Pochettino might be walking his dog – a Rhodesian Ridgeback called Sansa, named after the Game of Thrones character Sansa Stark – and the odd supporter would happily stop him to have a cosy chat. But he was always going to struggle to win over the supporters in their entirety.

He once said the first time he felt a connection with Chelsea’s supporters was in April 2024 after defeating Erik Ten Hag’s United 4-3, when Cole Palmer scored twice in the 10th and 11th minutes of stoppage time. That was 11 months after he joined.

He never quite won over the fanbase of Chelsea, where his football was chaotic and his high-intensity values led to accusations that he had worsened their injury crisis

One source at the time said Pochettino wanted ‘machines’ who had the physicality to play the high-energy philosophy he craved, and like at Spurs there was indeed a great deal of high-intensity running involved in training.

However, this talk of his sessions being fitness-focused led to accusations that his methods were contributing to their crippling injury list. Pochettino disputed that, telling us he did not come ‘from Mars’ and that he knew how to manage footballers better than those on social media. He was extremely defensive whenever asked if his training was primitive.

It would be fair to debate whether United have the players to play this way – and indeed how Pochettino himself would respond to the changing landscape of the Premier League.

Spurs boss Roberto de Zerbi noted recently that upon his return to the Premier League after two years away that almost all clubs now play a more physical game than when he was at Brighton. With more teams doing the same thing that once made a Pochettino side different, how would he adapt?

We are told leaving his job in charge of the USA is more contractually feasible now than it was before the 2026 World Cup when Spurs made checks last season. He has a buyout clause, apparently worth around £7million, though that does not include the compensation required to recruit Perez and Co.

Should United require any character references, they need only ask their own Luke Shaw. He wrote the epilogue of Guillem Balague’s book Brave New World: Inside Pochettino’s Spurs, having played under him at Southampton. Shaw admitted in those pages that he would love to work with his old coach again someday. Pochettino was there for him when Shaw broke his leg – still a man-manager even when they were no longer working together.

But United could also ask any number of Chelsea players who worked with Pochettino. They largely loved him. At the time of his dismissal in May 2024, one agent of a senior figure in the changing room told us that their client was ‘devastated’. Nicolas Jackson, formerly of Chelsea and now of Aston Villa, responded to Pochettino leaving by posting two face-palm emojis on Instagram.

Pochettino had his favourites. Conor Gallagher was one of them, and the Cobham graduate's contractual situation seemed to be a source of angst between the coach and Chelsea’s hierarchy.

Players tend to love Pochettino - Luke Shaw (right), one of Manchester United's veterans, had a strong relationship with him at Southampton

His power waned at Chelsea - the club hired a set-piece coach after he insisted he didn't want one, and he was gone before the specialist arrived

As noted, Pochettino was a builder hired to work with one of the Premier League’s youngest squads but did not get the time he wanted to mould Chelsea and never hid his desire for more power at Stamford Bridge. It is said they once had the chance to sign Ansu Fati from Barcelona on favourable financial terms, but did not go through with the transfer after the manager decided he was not for him.

We did get a glimpse of Pochettino’s waning power when Daily Mail Sport asked him once whether he would like a set-piece specialist adding to his staff. He dismissed the idea, suggesting he did not need one. Chelsea then lost the Carabao Cup final when Liverpool’s Virgil van Dijk headed in the winner in extra time from a corner, with Gary Neville coining the ‘blue billion-pound bottlejobs’ jibe.

A month later, Chelsea agreed a deal to hire Bernardo Cueva from Brentford to lead a new department dedicated to set-pieces. Pochettino responded by reminding us: ‘I am the head coach and I am going to decide if some people are going to be with me or not, or if I’m going to add more people or not to the touchline.’ He was gone before Cueva arrived in the summer.

An end-of-season review was held in May 2024, and Pochettino, along with Chelsea’s hierarchy, decided after a single season that it was not working. Not for him, and not for them.

Now those at the helm of United need to determine whether he is the man to bring the good vibes back, perhaps also with a little meat.

#1515. Roma prepare new contract for Donyell Malen

Donyell Malen continues to score, and Roma is preparing to reward him with a new contract.

The Dutch striker, a key figure in 2026, could soon sit down with the club to discuss a renewal accompanied by a salary increase.

According to Il Romanista, discussions had already been planned upon his arrival in the capital last January. Now, given the results he’s achieved, all the conditions are in place to keep that promise. When he left Aston Villa, Malen agreed to move to Roma while maintaining the same salary he earned in England.

However, the parties parted ways with the commitment to renegotiate the financial terms if the Dutchman’s performances justified an increase. And the numbers have exceeded expectations: according to the newspaper, Malen has scored 23 league goals in the 2026 calendar year, more than any other player in the five major European tournaments.

The transformation has largely been driven by the insights of Gian Piero Gasperini. In Rome, Malen has found the consistency as a centre-forward that he lacked in Birmingham, where he was often deployed on the wing. His relationship with the manager is excellent, and the player has repeatedly expressed his satisfaction with his time with the Giallorossi. This season, he has already scored 12 goals for Roma, confirming the form he showed in the second half of last season.

The striker’s performance hasn’t gone unnoticed abroad either. According to Il Romanista, interest is starting to pour in from other leagues, further motivating Roma to secure a player who has become central to their coaching project. However, no specific clubs have been named, nor is there a concrete offer on the table.

The negotiations are still underway, but the mood is described as positive. Malen wants to continue in the capital, and Roma has every interest in developing one of their key players. Before returning to Trigoria, the Dutchman will be playing tomorrow against Germany in the Nations League, after finding the net again for his national team in the 7-0 win over Greece. He will then resume his pursuit of Gasperini, while the club prepares the groundwork for a new agreement.

#1514. Roma could choose to terminate Dovbyk’s loan at Bologna

Artem Dovbyk’s future could change again during the season.

The Ukrainian striker, who moved from Roma to Bologna during the last summer transfer window, has so far failed to establish himself at the Emilian club.

His record shows only one goal, accompanied by performances that have not fully met expectations. His coaching relationship with Raffaele Palladino also appears to have failed to produce the desired results, fueling rumors of a possible early end to his time at the Rossoblu.

The situation will be discussed between the two clubs.

According to Il Messaggero, a meeting is scheduled between Bologna and Roma in the coming days to evaluate the striker’s position. The Bolognese club is reportedly considering terminating the loan before its due date, given the player’s difficulties.

A possible separation, however, will not depend solely on Bologna’s wishes, as the agreements signed during the summer include specific conditions for changing the striker’s destination.

The key issue concerns the transfer formula itself. The contract stipulates that only Roma can decide to terminate Dovbyk’s loan early, thus maintaining control over the Ukrainian’s eventual return to the capital. Bologna would not be able to unilaterally terminate the agreement, but would need to obtain the Giallorossi’s consent.

This clause requires an agreement between the parties before any changes are made and gives Roma a key role in the upcoming evaluations. Another crucial factor will be the possible future of Dovbyk. Without a club willing to welcome the striker, it appears unlikely that Roma will agree to amend the current agreements.

The Giallorossi will need to evaluate possible solutions, including based on their own transfer needs, avoiding a return without concrete prospects. The meeting with Bologna will serve to clarify the intentions of the two clubs, but an early termination of the loan remains, for now, only a possibility. The Ukrainian’s future will therefore depend on the opportunities that may arise in the coming weeks.

#1509. 18 more England records Harry Kane could break after becoming all-time caps leader

Harry Kane. The most-capped England player of all time and the top scorer for his country too. He might just be his nation’s best ever representative, you know.

Sure, he wasn’t around for the World Cup win in 1966. But when that’s the only major honour England have ever won, you can’t exactly knock players down for not replicating it.

With someone like Kane, you just have to look at the numbers to realise what he’s achieved. More often than not, he passes the eye test as well. He’s been a huge influence for England at some tournaments over the years.

And now, after his cap against Croatia on Thursday, he’s played in more England internationals than anyone else. A whole 126 of them.

Kane can proudly boast the all-time appearance and goal records for England, which are the big two. He also holds the records for most appearances as captain, most appearances at the Euros, most caps and goals while playing for a foreign club, most goals in a calendar year and so on.

But there are still more he could break. He’s 33 now, but still in good shape. Come on, this is the reigning Ballon d’Or winner we’re talking about.

So here are some records that could be in his sights over the rest of his international career.

Kane’s already a joint-record holder for this one and, unlike the three old-timers he shares the record with, he’s done it twice.

The record is six, first set by Tinsley Lindley in the 1880s and since matched by Jimmy Windridge in the 1900s, Tommy Lawton in the 1930s and Kane in both 2019 and between December 2022 and June 2023.

Steve Bloomer, from the 1890s, has the record of scoring in 10 consecutive appearances, but there were fixtures he didn’t play in in between.

So Kane is one of the four record holders for most consecutive England games scored in – and he’s not far off doing it for a third time.

He’s scored in every England game since the World Cup and so is currently on a run of five. All he needs to do is score against Spain on Sunday and then in England’s first game of the March international break to become the first man to score in seven consecutive England fixtures.

The next tournament England will be turning their attention to qualifying for is Euro 2028. And yes, they have to qualify, despite being co-hosts.

Kane is already a few days older than the current record holder for the oldest England scorer in a Euros qualifying match – Kyle Walker at 33 years and 104 days – and he’s going to score at least once in qualifying, right?

Should England make it to Euro 2028, you’d imagine Kane would still be an important player by then.

It’d be his fourth Euros with England, enough for him to overtake the eight players he’s currently level with. The only other among them still active in international football is Jordan Henderson, but we see Kane as a safer bet to be in the squad by then.

The next Euros would also be the seventh consecutive tournament Kane had represented England at. He’s currently tied with Henderson, Sol Campbell and Wayne Rooney on six in a row.

Kane will be 34 years and 317 days old when Euro 2028 kicks off. It won’t make him the oldest player to represent England at the tournament – that’s goalkeeper Peter Shilton at 38 – but he would be the oldest outfield player, presuming no one older than him would be in the squad.

Only Henderson and Dan Burn were older than him in the World Cup squad and we’d be a bit surprised if they were still sticking around for the next tournament.

The current record is held by Stuart Pearce at 34 years and 63 days old.

Surely Kane has at least one more goal in him at the Euros, even if we are looking 18 months into the future here.

If he does, he’d overtake Alan Shearer, who he’s currently tied with on seven, as England’s top scorer at the Euros. In fact, unless anyone was to get there before him, only Cristiano Ronaldo and Michel Platini would still be above him for the competition as a whole.

In the event of him scoring at Euro 2028, Kane would have a goal to his name from five consecutive international tournaments.

His only equivalent on four is Michael Owen.

And whenever that hypothetical Euros goal would come, Kane would be guaranteed to beat Trevor Brooking’s record as England’s oldest scorer at the competition.

Sir Trevor was 31 years old when he set the record, an age Kane is already past.

A bit more ambitious here, but the current record for most goals at a single Euros tournament by an Englishman is five, set by Alan Shearer in 1996.

It’s not that far out of reach, is it? Sure, only nine players have done it for any country before, but if England were to go far, there’d be enough games for Kane to have a crack at it.

He consistently steps up at the World Cup for his country and there’s no reason why he couldn’t at the Euros too. His personal best at the tournament is four in 2021, for the delayed 2020 edition.

And like Shearer in ’96, he’d have home advantage to carry him through as well.

File this one under unlikely, but maybe not as much as it sounds.

Onto the next tournament cycle and we could imagine a future in which Kane is still involved for the build-up to the 2030 World Cup.

He recently said it was “fairly realistic” that he’d still be an England player by the time of the next World Cup, but of course, England would have to get there first.

The current oldest scorer for England in a World Cup qualifying match is Teddy Sheringham, who was 35 years and 187 days old.

Details of the qualification process for the 2030 World Cup aren’t out yet, but Kane will turn 35 in the summer of 2028 and if he scores towards the end of a qualification campaign, he’d be able to surpass Sheringham.

If Kane does make it to the next World Cup, and plays for England at least once in every year in between, he’ll set a new record for the most consecutive years of appearances for the Three Lions.

2026 is the 12th consecutive year in which he’s appeared for his country. The record of 15 is currently shared by David Seaman and Rio Ferdinand.

As long as his England career continues uninterrupted, Kane will join them in 2029 and beat them in 2030.

Kane is already England’s top scorer at the World Cup, but he hasn’t played the most games at it for his country.

The record is Jordan Pickford’s with 19. Kane is one behind on 18.

There’s every chance both of them will be at the World Cup next time, but there’s half a suspicion Pickford could be phased out by then – especially if someone like James Trafford develops over the next few years.

A successor to Kane up front isn’t quite as obvious just yet and so he might be relied upon for longer, giving him a chance to overtake his long-time teammate.

The oldest scorer for England at a World Cup finals game was Tom Finney. He was 36 years and 64 days old when he scored against the Soviet Union in 1958.

Kane will be more than 250 days older than that by the time the next World Cup commences, so he’d just need a goal at any time to beat it.

Kane’s recent contract renewal with Bayern Munich means he’ll be playing in Germany until 2029.

He’s played for England 41 times since he left Tottenham Hotspur and the Premier League behind in 2023.

That means he only needs to play 14 more times to equal, or 15 times to beat, David Beckham’s record for the most caps earned while not playing club football in England.

55 of Beckham’s caps came after he left Manchester United to embark on a career with Real Madrid, LA Galaxy and AC Milan (he had retired from international football by the time he joined his last club, PSG).

You’d imagine Kane will play way more than 15 times for England between now and 2029.

Believe it or not, Kane hasn’t scored a hat-trick for England for five years now, last doing so in November 2021 against San Marino.

But it was his fifth international hat-trick and only Jimmy Greaves has more for England with six.

Could Kane get two more to overtake him? That might require some luck of the draw with qualifying for tournaments, pitting England against weaker teams, but he’s got enough time to try.

He does it often enough at club level, after all.

Even if he just gets one more hat-trick to match Greaves, he’d stand alone as the oldest hat-trick scorer for England.

That’s currently Jack Rowley at 31 years and 40 days old in 1949. It’s been a long-standing record, but Kane would instantly set a new one if he was to score an international hat-trick at any point from now.

Another one that might need some luck of the draw, but Kane has played seven times against Croatia in his England career, including on his record-breaking cap.

The only man to have played against a single, non-British opponent more is Alan Ball, who played eight times against West Germany between 1965 and 1975.

England and Croatia seem to meet every other week, so although the international schedule beyond this break remains unclear, there’s every chance Kane will cross paths with them again.

On a similar note, the most anyone has scored against a single non-British opponent for England is eight, by Vivian Woodward against Austria between 1908 and 1909.

Kane’s most common victims have been Albania (seven goals) and Croatia (six goals). If he plays against either of them again once or twice, he might fancy his chances.

#1508. Bloodthirsty Brighton feast on rattled Arsenal

Overpowered and overrun, Arsenal were subjected to the sort of gruelling treatment they usually inflict on their opponents. Mikel Arteta’s side did not look anything like Premier League champions here, as Brighton and Hove Albion produced a stunning performance full of swarming energy and breathless bravery.

In the biggest test of their season so far, Arsenal fell woefully short of the standards they have set themselves over the past few campaigns. This sort of thing simply does not happen to Arteta’s side. Well, it did not happen. Not before this monstering on the south coast, where the Brighton fans were whipped into a frenzy by the brilliance of Fabian Hürzeler’s players.

Brighton were everything that Arsenal are expected to be: aggressive, inventive and dominant across the field. They even scored with a set-piece, as one of Arsenal’s great strengths became a sudden weakness. Everywhere Arteta looked, the foundational truths of his team were being shaken by a Brighton storm. It was their first defeat by a three-goal margin since May 2023, also against Brighton.

Remarkably, this is now the third consecutive season in which Brighton have beaten the reigning Premier League champions. They are rarely happier than when they are on the hunt against more illustrious opponents, working as a team to snap at heels and then attacking in numbers. They are known as the Seagulls, but they played more like a pack of bloodthirsty wolves. The ferocity of their off-the-ball work, especially in the first half, was extraordinary.

Not for a long time have Arsenal been as rattled as they were here. David Raya misplaced passes, Gabriel Magalhães lost duels and Bruno Guimarães chased the ball in vain. It was Brighton’s Pascal Gross, rather than Arsenal’s Martin Odegaard, who shaped the game in midfield. It was Brighton’s Charalampos Kostoulas, rather than Arsenal’s Kai Havertz, who offered incisive class in attack.

Gross and Kostoulas both struck from range in a one-sided first half, before Chema Andrés added the third after the break. At half-time, Arteta had sprinted down the tunnel towards the dressing room. Whatever messages he gave to his players, they either did not sink in or did not work. By the end, Arsenal were lucky the scoreline was not even more humiliating.

Arteta’s players had come through some tricky assignments in winning their first seven matches of this season, but this was their toughest test yet and they failed it badly. They did not handle the emotions of the occasion particularly well, either: in stoppage time, a frustrated Declan Rice kicked out at Malick Yalcouyé. He was perhaps fortunate to avoid a red card.

It was the first time that Rice and Guimarães had started alongside each other for Arsenal and it quickly became clear that their £180m partnership will need some work. Arsenal would have hoped their experience in the Premier League would allow for an instant connection but, evidently, that is not the case. Guimarães was hooked after 60 minutes, but might easily have been removed at the break.

Both managers had a similar assessment of the match and how it was won: Brighton did the basics far better than Arsenal. “How we wanted to approach this game was getting into it through small wins,” Hürzeler said. “Everyone speaks about a goal or chance as a win, but a small win can be the first throw-in, the first corner, win the first header, win the first tackle. These small things. If you win these small steps, and celebrate them as a win, then you can gain bigger and bigger wins.”

It was typical of Brighton that one of their new signings produced an excellent performance in midfield. Andrés, a 21-year-old Spaniard signed from Stuttgart at the end of the transfer window, looks to be the latest gem identified by their data-led recruitment model. No one inside the Amex Stadium was thinking about Carlos Baleba, sold to Manchester United, when Andrés made his tackles and won his headers.

Another new signing, centre-back Luka Vuskovic, was similarly impressive at the back. Signed for £46m from Tottenham Hotspur, Vuskovic looks more than capable of going to the top of the game.

This was perhaps the first occasion this season in which Arsenal missed William Saliba, the injured centre-back who has been so fundamental to their success in recent years. The Frenchman can always be relied on to provide calmness and composure at the back, even under intense pressure. Without him, Arsenal were uncharacteristically jittery.

“The amount of technical errors we did in our own half...” Arteta bemoaned. “We didn’t respect any principle of play that you have to get out of those man-to-man situations. That put us always on the back foot.”

Gross, who at 35 is playing as well as ever, opened the scoring with a low shot from range after 31 minutes. Kostoulas then struck the second, from a similar distance, after some end-to-end action resulted in Arsenal’s midfield and defence melting away. The third was the most simple, as Andrés headed in at the back post from an inswinging corner.

Arsenal did have some chances, with Havertz missing the best of them, but there was never a sense that Brighton were vulnerable. The pressure on the home side was never sustained. For Arteta, who now has an extended international break in which to ruminate on this defeat, it all made for an unfamiliar and unexpected pain.

Mikel Arteta said his Arsenal players failed to “respect the game” as their perfect start to the season was ended in stunning style by a brilliant Brighton performance.

Arsenal’s capitulation on the south coast led to their first defeat of the campaign and Arteta admitted that Brighton had a different “edge” and “bite” throughout the match. The Arsenal manager also said the 3-0 loss represented a “big lesson” for his players.

“There are certain basics you need to accomplish in football, especially in the Premier League, that we were very far from,” Arteta said. “From the first throw-in you could sense it, it was so clear.

“It was a really disappointing result and performance. Brighton were another gear up from us. We were extremely poor technically and were not respecting the game.

“It is not going to take away what the team has done in the last six or seven weeks since coming back from the World Cup. What we have done and the way we have competed, and the amount of games we have won, has been remarkable. But this is a big lesson for all of us to understand what it takes to win at this level.”

Arteta added that his team did not “respect the principles of play” that were required against Brighton’s intense pressing, and also said his players were guilty of numerous technical errors.

“Credit to Brighton for what they have done because they have overcome us and they had another edge,” Arteta said. “There are a lot of moments when the ball is 50/50 and it changes hands and most of the time it was for them.”

Brighton are the Premier League’s top scorers this season with 16 goals in five matches so far, and this emphatic victory took them up to third place in the table.

“It was a special win,” Fabian Hürzeler, the Brighton head coach, said. “Not only because we played the best team in England but because of the performance. I am really proud of my team. It’s always important to enjoy these moments. We were horrible to play against. My players really trust each other on the pitch.”

Two things, one give credit to them. In the manner that they played and committed to every single action. We were below the standards that are required for us but in the Premier League as well.

When you miss chances like we did it becomes impossible. I want to congratulate Brighton for what they’ve done. It’s a big lesson for us to learn. If I have to describe how the team has played and competed in the last six or seven weeks, has been expectational but today has been a big lesson.

A very disappointing result and performance. Full credit to Brighton the manner they went about the game, they were a different gear from us. We didn’t do the basics right for long periods, especially in the first half. We didn’t win enough duels, and any second balls and that stretches you.

We were poor technically when we had the ball in our own half, we didn’t apply the principles that you need against a team that wants to press you man to man.

Arteta: "There are certain basics that you need to accomplish in the Premier League that we were very far from. The amount of technical errors we did... we didn't respect any principle of play. We were always on the back foot. They had another edge."

Beating the current champions and maybe the best team in England is something special. The result is nice but the performance is what makes it special, the boys showed real courage, real intensity and they were horrible to play against because we did the basics right.

Intensity, intensity, winning the personal duels...we have to have the belief to compete with the best teams in the league. My players really trust each other on the pitch. If one player is out then another can replace him.

Overall we wanted to be really good in every phase. We needed to be at the highest level. We go game by game. After the international break we have a lot of games. After wins like this we have to stay humble and understand why we had this win. We have to keep on going.

Our 125 anniversary & one of the best days! 💫 pic.twitter.com/YbZLTFPpWN

I thought we showed great intensity, waited for mistakes and punished Arsenal. It was a strong performance, a very complete performance.

We won the ball high up and attacked really fast. After the last two wins we are full of confidence and wanted to finish really strong before the international break.

I feel really good. I can’t complain. I just try to help the team when I can. I really enjoy life in Brighton, I’m loving it.

I know after the international break we play every three days and a lot of the lads are not used to that. It will be tough. I hope we can compete. We have a big squad this season.

Very excited for this one today. Arsenal have won all seven of their matches so far. Only once before in their history have they won their first eight games of a season - that was in 1903, when they were playing in the Second Division as Woolwich Arsenal. pic.twitter.com/iNBxoHl4Gc

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of today’s Premier League 3pm kick-offs, with Brighton vs Arsenal the pick of the three matches.

Brighton are the league’s top goalscorers so far this season and have amassed the most expected goals, but the champions have the league’s best defence and are seeking five wins from five to start their title defence. There is some welcome needle between Fabian Hurzeler and Mikel Arteta, dating back to Declan Rice’s contentious second yellow for delaying the restart two years ago, as well as the Brighton manager’s comments about Arsenal’s style of play in March.

That 1-0 Arsenal victory at the Amex coincided with Man City dropping points at home to Nottingham Forest on a pivotal night in the title race. Bukayo Saka scored a deflected shot in the ninth minute, and Arsenal held on from there in an ugly but resolute display.

With Saka, Martin Odegaard and Kai Havertz fit and firing, as well as the introduction of Myles Lewis-Skelly and Bruno Guimaraes to Arteta’s midfield stable, Arsenal’s football has been more technical and enterprising so far this season. Brighton are one of the few teams who will back themselves to play through Arsenal’s press, which should make for an absorbing game.

Elsewhere, Newcastle are looking to bounce back from their shellacking at Leeds at home to surprise package Hull City. Mattias Jaissle’s team took four points from Liverpool and Spurs but there is concern about how many shots they are conceding. Hull remain unbeaten and continue to confound the odds and underlying data, but that surely cannot last forever.

Everton are also one of the division’s unbeaten teams, but will be targeting three points from a home game against Ipswich after three consecutive draws. Ipswich are sitting comfortably on six points after their win at Crystal Palace, though they did have the extra man for the majority at Selhurst Park.

#1507. Roma and Milan to battle it out over Mastantuono

The future of Franco Mastantuono could become one of the most interesting topics of the upcoming summer transfer window.

The Argentine talent, born in 2007 and owned by Real Madrid, is having a positive experience with Fiorentina, where he arrived on loan. His performances have attracted the attention of several Italian clubs, including Roma and AC Milan, who are interested in assessing his availability for next season.

According to today’s edition of La Repubblica, Fiorentina believes they have a good chance of retaining Mastantuono next season.

Sporting director Fabio Paratici is reportedly working to ensure continuity in the Argentine’s development, as he has quickly become an important member of the team.

His performances confirm his impact: he has already scored four goals in Italy, along with a central role in the team’s technical decisions. This performance strengthens the Tuscan club’s position vis-à-vis Los Blancos, who own his contract and are tasked with deciding on the player’s next destination.

The interest of Roma and Milan is a factor not to be underestimated in defining the future of the 2007-born player. Both clubs have reportedly already begun exploring the prospect ahead of next season, evaluating the possibility of joining the race for the Argentine talent.

His ability to make an impact in attack and his young age make him a particularly attractive prospect for clubs looking to invest in promising players. At the moment, however, no advanced negotiations have been reported, only expressions of interest and preliminary evaluations.

#1506. The top goalscorers for club & country in 2026 so far: Kane, Yamal, Mbappe, Raphinha…

Big names from Real Madrid, Barcelona, Arsenal and Bayern Munich feature alongside some surprise names in the most prolific goalscorers of the calendar year so far.

Some big names are surprisingly absent from the most prolific goalscorers of 2026 to date.

Drawn from Europe’s five major leagues, here are the top 10 goalscorers in 2026 across club and international competitions.

Dembele has scored 20 goals in 36 PSG appearances this year, including several crucial strikes in Europe – none bigger than the equalising spot kick he coolly dispatched against Arsenal in the Champions League final.

His goal in France’s World Cup win over Iraq was, incredibly, his first in major tournament football. That was swiftly followed up with a rapid hat-trick against Norway, before another in the quarter-final against Morocco.

He is largely taking it easy right now, once again frequently rested during PSG’s domestic campaign. But he popped up with a goal against Manchester City.

Schick has had reason to celebrate in 2026. Earlier this year, he reached the milestone of 100 goals for Bayer Leverkusen.

He’s been on fire this season, with 12 goals from 14 games for the German side.

There won’t be any more international goals from Schick, though. He retired from Czech Republic duty after the World Cup.

The jury is still out on Gyokeres, who remains a perplexing forward.

This calendar year has seen him look borderline anonymous and increasingly sidelined at Arsenal.

And yet Gyokeres also fired Sweden to the World Cup with a hat-trick against Ukraine and a late winner against Poland. He’s basically the Ikea Gerd Muller at this point.

What a year it’s been for Malen. Started it as a benchwarmer at Aston Villa. Set to finish it as one of Europe’s most lethal strikers at Roma.

Malen made an immediate impact after his January move to the Italian capital and his scoring rate has barely slowed down since.

For some reason, his form hasn’t quite translated into international football; he hasn’t scored for the Netherlands at all this year.

But high-flying Roma are laughing. Malen almost won the Serie A golden boot last season despite arriving midway through and he’s a leading contender for the gong this season.

A fairly recent entrant into the top 10 after heading into the international break on the back of a hat trick against Union Berlin.

Olise was the Bundesliga’s best assister last season but has been more than capable of finding the net himself a fair few times too.

He didn’t score any goals at the World Cup but netted the winner in Zinedine Zidane’s second game in charge of France. The best Fantasy Footballer around right now.

Yamal has long been talked up as a Ballon d’Or contender, and slowly but surely he’s getting the numbers to back it up.

The teenager’s goalscoring output has grown season on season, and 2025-26 was no exception. February’s hat-trick against Villarreal was evidence of a player about to go truly stratospheric.

Unfortunately, the final furlong of the campaign was hit by a hamstring injury, or else we suspect he’d be a few places higher up in this list.

He needed just 10 minutes in his first World Cup start to find the back of the net, although that would be his only goal in Spain’s triumph out in North America.

Now he’s looking fit and hungry – at least based on the evidence of his exceptional form of late.

The Brazilian has an exceptional tally of 33 goals for Barcelona so far this calendar year (plus one for Brazil), which is especially impressive when you consider he’s missed quite a lot of action due to injury.

He averages a goal every 49 minutes for Barca this season – to put that in context, Kylian Mbappe averages a goal every 84 minutes for Real Madrid.

Raphinha has scored in all but three of the Barca games he’s played in in 2026-27, scoring hat tricks in two, and currently leads the Europe-wide goalscoring charts with 15 in the league.

The top three are the last three winners of the European Golden Shoe. This list has taken a while to take shape, but the frontrunners are the usual suspects.

Haaland’s four goals against Iraq and Senegal in the group stages finally saw him climb up into the top 10, from which he was surprisingly absent in the latter half of the 2025-26 club season, before he added to his World Cup tally against the Ivory Coast. Then there were two goals against Brazil.

He finally drew a blank as Norway exited the World Cup at the hands of England at the quarter-final stage. He earned a well-deserved rest before spearheading Man City’s new era under Enzo Maresca.

Same as it ever was with nine goals in nine Premier League appearances for City this season, plus braces against Porto and PSG and another Champions League goal against his favourite opponents, RB Leipzig.

Like his rival Haaland, it somehow took Mbappe until mid-June to enter the top 10.

Mbappe kicked off the year in superb style, scoring in six successive starts for Real Madrid (nine goals in total) before dipping considerably with just one goal in his next seven appearances.

By the nature of his 10 goals at the World Cup, we don’t expect to see the Real Madrid superstar dropping back out. His Champions League record is pretty sensational.

Arguably the finest player in world football right now. How often have you been able to say that about an Englishman?

The only player in Europe’s five major leagues to average a better-than-goal-a-game output so far this calendar year, the England captain has 41 goals in 40 appearances for Bayern Munich in all competitions in 2026 – including home and away against Real Madrid and PSG.

He capped off his superb season with a hat-trick in the DFB Pokal final. Two goals against Croatia showed Kane carried his form into the World Cup, where he eventually scored six times.

Unbelievably, the Norway game was Kane’s first knockout appearance for club and country in 2025-26 in which he didn’t score. Which, of course, he followed with a blank against Argentina.

Surprisingly enough, Kane failed to add to his tally by drawing a blank in his first three Bayern appearances of the 2026-27 campaign.

But it’s back to normal service with his Bayern tally standing at 10 goals in 14 games. The Czechs and Croatia have been on the receiving end in the Nations League too.

Still some way to go before catching Lionel Messi’s calendar year record, mind.

Roma is ready to secure Mario Hermoso, who has become a key figure in Gian Piero Gasperini’s squad.

After a difficult period that kept him away from the Giallorossi project for approximately six months, the Spanish defender has completely turned his situation around. In the summer of 2025, his stay in the capital seemed far from certain, with the real possibility of a separation.

Today, however, Hermoso is considered a key element in the Roma squad’s stability, so much so that he is close to reaching a new contract.

According to La Gazzetta dello Sport, a renewal could be reached as early as next week.

Gasperini has transformed a player considered on his way out into one of the team’s leaders, leveraging his experience and technical skills.

#1504. Where are they now? England’s XI that beat Spain 3-2 in the 2018 Nations League

England’s Nations League win over Spain in October 2018 was one of the best away results achieved by the national team in the 21st century.

In a game famous for Eric Dier’s totally-got-the-ball challenge on Sergio Ramos, Gareth Southgate’s team raced into a 3-0 lead before clinging on for victory.

As the Three Lions travel to Spain once more, we’ve looked back eight years and investigated what that XI is doing today.

Pickford has been England’s No.1 for over eight years, although this status is now threatened by the emergence of James Trafford.

The Everton goalkeeper has seen off challenges from Aaron Ramsdale, Nick Pope, Sam Johnstone and Dean Henderson, becoming a stalwart at five successive major tournaments.

He’s still in good form at club level, but there were signs over the summer that Pickford may be starting to wane. Euro 2028 is feasible, but probably not the next World Cup.

A late bloomer, Trippier’s England debut didn’t arrive until he was nearly 27 in a friendly against France in June 2017.

Despite tough competition at right-back, Trippier became a stalwart of the Southgate era. He won 54 caps and scored that famous free-kick against Croatia in the semi-finals.

He’s now playing in the Championship with Wolves, who are handily placed to return to the top flight at the first time of asking.

Gomez would’ve probably won more than 15 international caps had he remained injury-free throughout his career.

But the centre-back remains at Liverpool in 2026 and his penalty in the recent Carabao Cup shootout win over Chelsea bought the house down at Anfield. Gomez has never scored in his professional career, but remains a popular member of the team.

Once the most expensive centre-back in world football, it was Maguire’s England heroics that really made his name.

The centre-back was still at Leicester City when he lined up in Seville eight years ago, but his reputation was blossoming and a move to Manchester United came the following summer.

Maguire is still at Old Trafford in 2026, now working under his sixth permanent manager in Mauricio Pochettino.

But he’s not played for England much under Thomas Tuchel, limited to appearances in friendlies against Uruguay and Japan in March.

An international recall looks unlikely as younger alternatives have emerged, coupled with Maguire losing what little pace he had.

Like Maguire, Chilwell was building his reputation at Leicester at the time of this match. He earned a £45million move to Chelsea in 2020 and won the Champions League a year later.

At international level, Chilwell was generally second choice behind Luke Shaw. He only played four times after 2021, the last appearance coming in a friendly against Belgium two-and-a-half years ago.

His form at Chelsea slipped and the left-back was farmed out to Strasbourg. The 29-year-old now plays for Crystal Palace.

Years before he became a hate figure at Leicester, Winks was considered one of those neat and tidy midfielders essential for international success.

But his international career was halted by the rise of Declan Rice, a much more traditional English midfielder and also, crucially, a lot better.

Then at Spurs, Winks played his final England game in 2020. Having been relegated two years in a row with Leicester, he escaped this summer and now plays in Italy for Cagliari.

If seeing Winks in this XI produces a double-take, then his replacement in Seville is surely even more surprising.

Chalobah racked up a total of six minutes and 54 seconds for his country, one second more than Martin Kelly who holds the record for the shortest England career.

Southgate loved the player from his Under-21 days, but Chalobah never looked likely to become a senior regular and now plays for Charlton Athletic in the Championship.

Dier had two crowning moments at international level – his penalty against Colombia at the 2018 World Cup and the aforementioned banjaxing of Ramos.

However, the former Spurs man hasn’t played for his country since 2022 and is now out in Ligue 1 for Monaco.

No matter how many times Barkley pops up for Aston Villa, it’s still a surprise to see him playing at such a high level.

Not because he’s untalented. But Barkley has been around forever and didn’t seem the type of player to enjoy this level of longevity. Especially as he last played for England in October 2019.

Walker, his replacement against Spain, won the last of his 96 caps in the 3-1 loss to Senegal last year.

He’d dramatically lost form at Manchester City and the 36-year-old captains struggling Burnley in the second tier.

Sterling scored twice in this game and was an important player for Southgate’s England right up until the 2022 World Cup.

He won the last of his 82 caps during that tournament before entering a decline. First, he was spat out by Chelsea and had unsuccessful spells at Arsenal and Feyenoord.

In May 2026, Sterling was arrested on suspicion of drug-driving after being found under the influence of nitrous oxide. He admitted the charge in September and is due to appear in court at the end of this month.

Still only 31, his career in elite football appears over.

It’s easy to forget that Rashford is still only 29 years old, having made his England debut over 10 years ago. He also scored on this night in Seville as England claimed a notable scalp.

Having eventually been overwhelmed by the dysfunction at Manchester United, Rashford spent time out on loan at Aston Villa and Barcelona.

His good form for the La Liga champions earned him a spot in this year’s World Cup squad, scoring against Croatia in the group stage.

But Barcelona chose to sign Anthony Gordon instead, leading to an awkward return to United. You could see Pochettino loving the player or choosing to sell him to signify a fresh start.

On the other hand, Rashford is well-liked by Tuchel and only missed out on the current squad through injury.

England’s captain, Ballon d’Or winner, record goalscorer and now all-time leading appearance maker, Kane is still leading the line for his country.

But there is trepidation over the national team’s Kane-less future, given he’s 33 and still hasn’t really delivered in the biggest knockout games.

A question to ponder, but one that will surely be delayed until after hosting Euro 2028.

#1503. Sarina Wiegman receives honorary damehood from Prince William at Windsor Castle - after leading Lionesses to back-to-back European titles

Published: 14:28 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 19:04 EST, 10 November 2026

Lionesses manager Sarina Wiegman has been awarded an honorary damehood by Prince William after leading England to back-to-back Euro wins.

Wiegman is Dutch and therefore cannot be made a substantive dame. Instead she has picked up the honorary title, because the Netherlands does not have a British monarch as its head of state.

She said upon being awarded the title at Windsor Castle on Tuesday: 'I feel very privileged to receive my honorary Damehood from His Royal Highness The Prince of Wales at Windsor Castle today.

'It is a day I will never forget and made even more special by sharing it with members of my family.

'I would like to again express my sincere gratitude for this honour and for the continued respect and warmth I experience from the English people. I thank everyone for their support.'

Wiegman was named in the King's New Year's Honours list at the end of 2025, alongside several members of her England team.

England manager Sarina Wiegman (left) has been awarded an honourary damehood by Prince William (right)

Captain Leah Williamson was awarded a CBE, with Alex Greenwood, Keira Walsh, Georgia Stanway and Ella Toone all being honoured with MBEs.

Wiegman said at the time: 'I would like to express my sincere gratitude for this honour. When I first arrived in England, I could never have imagined the respect and warmth I've experienced from the English people. I deeply thank the fans for their support.

'This title is a reflection of my exceptional team of players and staff. My congratulations go to Alex, Ella, Georgia, Keira, Leah and also Dr Ritan Mehta who have all been celebrated for their brilliant contributions.

'Our team values mean that when there is recognition for one, then there is recognition for all. I want to pay tribute to every member of our EURO squad. They should all be celebrated for everything they brought to the pitch and for the positive role they play in society. I'm proud to work alongside such a dedicated group of people.'

The former Netherlands coach took over the England team in 2021 and led them to success at Euro 2022 and Euro 2025.

She also reached the World Cup final in 2023, and signed a new two-year contract extension earlier this year, which will take her to the end of the 2029 Euros.

#1502. When Gus Poyet scored the goal of a lifetime yet Zola still stole the glory

Gus Poyet scored a lot of great goals for Chelsea, but in August 1999 he scored the best of all against Sunderland. Although, typically, Gianfranco Zola kind of stole the show.

Opening days of the season, just like final days, are often home to the bizarre, so much so that we might as well treat them as standalone events with little bearing on either the Premier League or football in general.

In 2011, Blackpool thumped Wigan Athletic 4-0 away from home, with Marlon Harewood running the show, but the Seasiders were ultimately relegated while the Latics stayed afloat – and Harewood ended the campaign on loan at Barnsley.

In 1996 a Fabrizio Ravanelli hat-trick was the start of something great for Middlesbrough, but nine months later they were dropping down to the second tier.

And in August 1999, Gianluca Vialli’s Chelsea were tipped as title contenders, thanks in no small part to an opening-day victory highlighted by the sort of goal you only normally see on adverts. Yet Vialli’s men did not even end up making the top four.

Back in the mid-90s, we weren’t exactly accustomed to South American footballers in the Premier League.

The number of players from the continent to appear in the competition was still in single figures, with Juninho and Faustino Asprilla the highest-profile, and not a single South American had turned out for any of the Premier League’s London clubs until Gustavo Poyet arrived at Chelsea in the summer of 1997.

The make-up of the division had changed greatly by the time he left the club in 2001, but while Poyet was no longer a novelty by then, he made his mark with 49 goals in the intervening years.

Zola's chipped assist 😲Poyet's volleyed finish 😍#GoalOfTheDay is a @ChelseaFC stunner pic.twitter.com/jkj3qY8BXH

— Premier League (@premierleague) February 18, 2020

For what might be the only time ever, you couldn’t dismiss this goal with the usual get-out of “come on, it’s only Sunderland”.

This was the season in which Kevin Phillips won the Premier League Golden Boot and the Black Cats finished seventh in the league, their highest placing in Poyet’s lifetime and comfortably higher than the 14th place to which he led the club in his spell as manager.

Yet the goal he scored in August 1999, his second of the game, felt more like the sort of strike you’d see from league champions rounding off their season against an already-relegated opponent.

In 1999 we were still at the stage of not entirely trusting defenders with their distribution, but even back then it was possible to tell the difference between a hopeful punt and a pass from deep. This was undoubtedly the latter.

Having said that, when you have Gianfranco Zola to aim at, can any ball really be called hopeful? Sure, Sunderland had men tracking the Italian, but they were mostly just for show – the ball was always destined to come under Zola’s spell

There were times at which the forward seemed to be playing a different game to the other 21 men on the pitch, and this was just a case of the ball arriving at his feet after little more than a saunter, with the opposition players knowing it would be harder for him to humiliate them if they kept their distance.

Tore Andre Flo was in support, coming short to receive, but in doing so he was making an unconscious decoy run he wouldn’t be able to identify until the ball was over his head.

It’s hard to think of too many goals in history where the flying scissor-volley isn’t the best part, but rules were made to be broken.

That’s right, Gus, I’m showing you up on your big day, but I’m sure you’ll understand. I mean, you effectively said as much yourself.

READ: A tribute to the wonderful Gianfranco Zola and his bargain move to Chelsea

“The only thing I know is Gianfranco Zola had the chance to pass it to me outside the box, but he showed me the way,” Poyet recalled in a 2015 interview.

“[It was] like saying don’t worry, just run, the ball is going to drop in front of you and then it’s up to you.”

Only the most special talents can see passes that aren’t even on the map, but look at who you’re dealing with here. Zola was a player capable of making his own team-mates better, even midfielders as talented and relatively prolific as Poyet.

As for the finish itself? The patience and precision of the build-up deserved – nay, needed something so emphatic, which makes Poyet’s own confusion all the more beautiful

“It’s something which I’ve never done before, I’ve never done after,” he said.

“It happened for some reason – no explanation.”

It’s as if Poyet had a temporary out-of-body experience, with someone else – Zola’s mind, perhaps – controlling his movements as he drove forward to reach a pass others won’t have even registered was being planned.

Sure, players will occasionally attempt over-elaborate volleys in training sessions, but those are shots to nothing, performed in the knowledge that if and when the moment arrives in an actual game it will more than likely be easier to just go for the simple finish.

We can only hope Poyet was only so seemingly unenthused when describing the goal in the interview above because he knew he was about to lose his job at the Stadium of Light.

Because, honestly, if you’d scored a goal like that you should want to talk about that and nothing else for the rest of your life.

#1498. The 8 players Barcelona let go in the summer – & how they’re faring elsewhere

When you get to play for a club like Barcelona, you probably don’t want to leave, but a few players had to this summer.

Barcelona have reclaimed their crown as La Liga’s best team over the past couple of years with Hansi Flick in charge. They boast one of the most talented squads in world football, but some members of that squad said goodbye in the summer.

Here are the first-team players who left Barcelona in the summer and how their next steps are going.

We did wonder if Barcelona might miss Lewandowski after letting his contract expire. The outstanding form of Raphinha has meant they’ve been just fine.

As for Lewandowski, who joined MLS side Chicago Fire as a free agent, a return of 10 goals from 23 games for his new club so far has been decent – if a little underwhelming compared to his usual standards.

He had an eight-game MLS goal drought across September and October, which is unthinkable for someone like him. Maybe Barcelona got out at the right time?

He is 38 now, to be fair. In Lewandowski’s defence, he has three goals from two games to his name in November ahead of the playoffs. It’d be silly to write him off.

It was a big summer for Torres, scoring the winner in the World Cup final and then joining the reigning Champions League holders PSG.

The 26-year-old scored a brace on his Ligue 1 debut and a hat-trick on his first Champions League appearance for his new club, before further league goals against Brest and Marseille.

But he went the entire run of eight games between the last international break and this one without scoring, so is stuck on seven goals from 14 games.

He’ll be happy with that as an overall ratio, but will be wanting to make his mark in more matches.

Those memories have become distant for Barcelona and they agreed last summer to send him on loan to Monaco with an option to buy.

After he scored 12 goals to make it his best goalscoring season yet, Monaco took up that option for €11m.

The winger’s start to this season has been disrupted by injuries though. He’s scored in both of his Conference League outings, but has only played three times in Ligue 1 since his permanent transfer.

It’s estimated he’ll be out for another month. What could he have been without the injuries?

Fort spent last season on loan away from Barcelona at Elche. Rather than getting a chance to come back and add to his 30 appearances, he was sold for a new challenge this summer.

Europa League participants Real Sociedad were the buyers. They’ve been patient with Fort so far; his first start against Bournemouth lasted just 45 minutes and he had to wait until after the first international break of the season for his first La Liga starts for his new club.

Still only 20, the Barcelona-born right-back is one for the future. What’s promising is that he made an assist within three minutes of his first league start for La Real against Malaga.

But he’s been an unused sub in three Europa League games since the Bournemouth loss.

Like Fort, Pena finished last season on loan with Elche. He headed further afield for his permanent move away, though, joining Greek giants Panathinaikos.

At the age of 27, it was probably about time for the goalkeeper to find a club to settle at. Panathinaikos looks to have been a good choice; he’s started 10 games in the Greek Super League so far and kept clean sheets in half of them.

Panathinaikos went into the international break sitting pretty at the top of the table.

Pena is yet to keep a clean sheet in their Conference League games, but he’s playing regularly in that competition too. An undisputed starter, which is pretty much what he’d have been hoping for.

After playing four times for Barcelona last season, young left-back Torrents made way for Ajax.

He’s only played once in the Eredivisie so far as a substitute before sitting on the bench for their next nine league games.

Still only 19, he’s had one start and one sub appearance in the Conference League.

Marques only played twice for Barcelona last season but he still went for €11m – the same price as Fati – when Braga bought him in the summer.

There’ll be high hopes for the 20-year-old midfielder in Portugal, but only one of his six games for Braga so far has been as a starter and even then he got taken off at half time.

Braga are in the Conference League this season, but Marques has been an unused sub in their games in it so far.

Cortes made his one and only Barcelona appearance against Alaves at the tail end of last season, lasting the full 90 minutes.

The left-footed centre-back was already 21 at the time and could probably tell he wasn’t part of the long-term plans, though.

He was sold to Royal Antwerp in the Belgian top flight and has settled in instantly, starting all eight of their games since his arrival.

#1497. Can you name the top scorers for these 25 European nations?

Many of club football’s greatest goalscorers can translate their form onto the international stage – but can you name the all-time leading goalscorers for these 25 European nations?

A combination of quality and longevity is key for anybody hoping to become their country’s record goalscorer and plenty of legendary figures have achieved just that.

With enlarged tournaments, a plethora of qualifiers and the UEFA Nations League, it’s perhaps inevitable that the list is dominated by more recent footballers.

The bar is set lower in some countries than others – we can’t be the only ones surprised that Italy’s record goalscorer only has 35 goals – but anybody who’s scored more for their country than anybody else is deserving of some respect.

And we’re asking you to name the record goalscorer for 25 of the most prominent European nations. You’ve got 15 minutes to name them all, and we must admit, this gets pretty tough in places.

We’ve given you the country and the number of goals as a clue and an asterisk denotes that they’re still active for their national team. There are some countries with joint record scorers but, in the spirit of kindness, we only require you to name one of them.

Once you’ve completed this quiz, try naming the most capped player for these 25 European nations?

#1495. Scott McTominay reveals hospital dash and heart shock treatment days before Scotland's World Cup opener

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 12:25 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 03:20 EST, 11 November 2026

Scott McTominay has revealed he needed a procedure to reset the beat of his heart just two days before Scotland’s World Cup campaign kicked off back in June.

Heading into the opening game against Haiti in Boston, the explanation given from the Scottish Football Association was that McTominay had been carrying a sickness bug.

But, after the squad had flown from their training base in Charlotte, McTominay had actually been whisked away to hospital straight from the airport via a police escort.

The 29-year-old had shock treatment on his heart before then going on to play all three games as Steve Clarke’s side were knocked out at the group stage.

The Napoli midfielder subsequently underwent corrective surgery back at the start of the season and missed Scotland’s opening four fixtures in the Nations League.

Now back in the squad ahead of the upcoming double-header with North Macedonia and Switzerland, McTominay has opened up for the first time on his health issues.

Scott McTominay had a heart procedure two days before playing against Haiti

Scott McTominay in action during Scotland's 1-0 World Cup win over Haiti

Asked about what happened, he replied: ‘The sickness bug? You’re not going to say I have something to do with my heart two days before the first game of the World Cup. It’s not an ideal scenario being in the hospital two days before — well, technically 36 hours before the first game of the World Cup.

‘But you have to take the cards you’re dealt on the chin. It’s part of the game. There’s nothing I could do about it and the shock went well, I was back in normal rhythm then 24 hours later you’re playing a World Cup game.

‘The World Cup, it was difficult for me, to be honest. I had to go and get the shock on my heart. That was two days before the Haiti game.

‘You prepare so well, I was in such good condition and something like that happens. You’re thinking: “How has this happened to me?” But then you have to get on with it. That’s the cards you are dealt in football.

‘Sometimes things don’t go your way and you have to continue to do your best. It’s nowhere near an excuse but it’s something you have to look back on and say: “Well, it’s part of the process”.

McTominay was given full reassurance from the doctors and medical staff that the procedure had gone well, insisting it was never in his thoughts to pull out of the squad.

Asked whether it was playing on his mind across the three games against Haiti, Morocco and Brazil, he said: ‘No. I put it to bed. I tried my best to put it to bed anyway. Whenever you go under anaesthetic and you have to get put to sleep, it decreases the athletic performance a little bit and sleep and stuff like that.

‘You have to get back round to doing it again. It was far from ideal but those are the cards that you’re dealt, there’s nothing you can do about it.’

Some fans had questioned McTominay’s form throughout the World Cup, oblivious to the fact that he was effectively playing through an ongoing heart issue.

Asked whether the criticism bothered him at the time, he continued: ‘It’s tough. It’s never easy, things like that, but you can’t use things like that as an excuse because that’s just not in my nature.

‘I take whole responsibility for a lot of the things that we didn’t create or didn’t score the goals in the World Cup.

‘I can put my face out there and say that that was nowhere near good enough. But that’s part of football. You have to get away and think about it and reflect and come back a better player.

‘I didn’t know that’s what people were saying. I probably had an idea.

‘I’ve been criticised a million times before in my career before but I don’t let it get under my skin or worry too much about it. You know yourself as a professional footballer if you’re not quite where you should be.

‘For me, I had half an idea but you just try to block it out because if you think about negative things you might speak it into existence.’
